title: The One Where Phoebe Runs

jokes.text: Rachel complains she got stuck with 'it's,' 'and,' and 'a' on the answering machine message while Phoebe got all the 'good words'
jokes.setup: Rachel and Phoebe are recording a shared answering machine greeting together, dividing up the words
jokes.punchline: 'I'm sorry, I have "a." Forget it.' — Rachel's indignation over getting only grammatical filler words is petty and perfectly in character
jokes.explanation: A charming cold open that uses a mundane real-world situation to reveal character instantly. Rachel's outrage over grammatical filler words is a recognizable type of petty vanity that suits her perfectly. The escalating specificity ('it's,' 'and,' 'a') lands well.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Okay, on three. One, two, three.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Hi, you've reached Rachel and Phoebe. We can't take your call right now.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Please leave a message after the beep.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Wait, why do you always get the good words?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: What are you talking about? I say 'beep.'

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You get 'message' and 'please.' I'm stuck with 'you've reached' and 'right now.'

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, I wanted to say 'reached.' That's a good word.

jokes.text: On the second attempt, Phoebe somehow ends up saying all the words including Rachel's assigned ones
jokes.setup: They switch words and try again; Rachel expects to say the substantive words this time
jokes.punchline: Phoebe still ends up saying everything — 'Hi... everybody... it's... Rachel... and... Phoebe's.' Rachel's bewildered 'Wait. How did you do that?' captures the absurdity
jokes.explanation: The best payoff of the cold open. The absurdity that Phoebe somehow took ALL the words even after the switch, plus Rachel's genuine bafflement ('Oh, you're no ordinary roommate, are you?'), is a tight three-beat escalation. Phoebe's quasi-supernatural social dominance is a great running character joke.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I also have the word 'a'. How thrilling for me.

jokes.text: While Rachel is gone, Phoebe re-records the message solo, stealing all the words: 'Hi, it's Phoebe and Rachel's. Please leave a message. Thanks!'
jokes.setup: Rachel has gone ahead to run; the answering machine dispute seemed settled
jokes.punchline: Phoebe immediately re-records it alone, putting her own name first and taking every single word — 'You've met your match, Rachel Greene!'
jokes.explanation: The perfect button on the cold open. Phoebe's gleeful declaration 'You've met your match, Rachel Greene!' is surprisingly quotable and reveals a competitive, mischievous streak that makes her more three-dimensional. The structure is excellent — the whole cold open built to this. High craft for a cold open gag.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You know what? You're right. That was silly of me. I'll switch.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: You take 'sophisticated' and 'exotic,' and I'll take 'bubbly' and 'fun.'

jokes.text: 'You've met your match, Rachel Greene!'
jokes.setup: Rachel has just realized Phoebe outmaneuvered her on the answering machine again
jokes.punchline: Phoebe delivers a triumphant villain monologue-style declaration over a petty answering machine dispute
jokes.explanation: A fun button to the opening bit. The disproportionate grandiosity ('You've met your match!') applied to something completely trivial is classic Phoebe. Good economy — four words do a lot of work.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God. Phoebe's been saying words this whole time.

jokes.text: Chandler finishes his book about computers achieving human brain capacity by 2030 and announces he realized he can sleep with his eyes open
jokes.setup: Chandler shares an impressive intellectual finding about computers matching human consciousness — the audience expects a philosophical or witty observation
jokes.punchline: 'And I just realized I can sleep with my eyes open.' — The cosmic irrelevance of Chandler's personal discovery after such a grand setup
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed misdirection: the camera lingers on Chandler delivering a genuinely interesting futurist premise, only to have him pivot to a useless personal discovery. The gap between the grand (AI consciousness) and the mundane (eye-open sleeping) is perfectly calibrated. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: We could go running together! It's great exercise and bonding time.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Running? I thought you said chasing men.

jokes.text: Monica discovers Chandler nailed the boxes to the floor — Chandler reveals he didn't, meaning they can be moved
jokes.setup: Monica compliments what she assumes is a clever organizational decision: 'Honey, it was a great idea, nailing the boxes to the floor'
jokes.punchline: 'I didn't nail the boxes to the floor.' / 'So you can move them!' — Monica's instant pivot from admiration to predatory efficiency
jokes.explanation: Monica's obsessive control-freak nature is on full display. The joke works because of perfect character integration — Monica's fleeting disappointment that the boxes AREN'T nailed down (she was relieved to have a reason not to move them) is replaced instantly by opportunistic drive. Very Monica.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I got her! I finally got her! She said 'hello', I said 'goodbye'. Game over, Rachel. Game over.

jokes.text: Chandler tries to escape Monica's moving request by pivoting: 'While I'm doing that, Ross has a great computer story for you'
jokes.setup: Monica has just realized the boxes can be moved and will clearly rope Chandler into helping
jokes.punchline: Chandler immediately tries to redirect to Ross's boring story as a distraction/deflection
jokes.explanation: A quick character beat — Chandler throwing Ross under the bus to avoid labor. It's functional and gets a smile, but it's a minor moment.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: It's fascinating, really. With quantum computing and neural mapping, theoretically we could download human consciousness into a digital substrate, achieving a form of digital immortality.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Wow, that's incredible.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I know, right? Imagine the possibilities—

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So when are you doing it?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Well, actually, I can't. I have a fear of computers.

jokes.text: Joey introduces Janine, then redundantly adds 'And she's gonna live with me!'
jokes.setup: Joey introduces Janine as his new roommate to the group
jokes.punchline: 'And she's gonna live with me!' — Joey states what 'roommate' already meant, as if it's a revelatory bonus fact
jokes.explanation: Classic Joey — he doesn't know that 'roommate' implies 'lives with me,' or he's so excited he's saying it twice just to process his own luck. Either reading is funny and deeply character-specific. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Chandler meets Janine and responds to learning her last name 'Le Croix' with 'I didn't know that. What a pretty last name.'
jokes.setup: Chandler asks Janine her last name as a normal social courtesy
jokes.punchline: 'I didn't know that. What a pretty last name.' — Chandler complimenting information he literally just received, as if he had any prior reason to know it
jokes.explanation: Chandler's social awkwardness expressed through grammatically correct but logically absurd politeness. It's a small but specific character moment — Chandler being weirdly formal in a way that reveals his discomfort.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Oh, I know what will cheer you up. Ross was telling me about the sedimentary layers he found in the park. It was fascinating!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, he's in the other room. I'll go get him.

jokes.text: When told Janine is from Australia, Chandler responds 'From the land down under?' and then 'I didn't know that either!' when told she's a dancer
jokes.setup: The group is making normal small talk with Janine; Chandler is clearly flustered by her attractiveness
jokes.punchline: Chandler's 'I didn't know that either!' after learning she's a dancer — he's not being sarcastic, he's genuinely processing information and announcing it like news bulletins
jokes.explanation: The running gag of Chandler announcing obvious-to-him new information works as a callback to the previous beat and builds a mini-pattern. His flustered state makes each 'I didn't know that' funnier than the last.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: This is my new roommate, Janine. She's a dancer.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: And just to be clear, she lives here. With me. In my apartment. We share the same living space.

jokes.text: Janine excuses herself to unpack; implied beat as the group watches her go
jokes.setup: Janine has just been introduced and exits to unpack
jokes.punchline: The implied collective male reaction — the audience sees all three men watching her leave, the silence speaking for itself before the dialogue about how beautiful she is
jokes.explanation: A standard multi-cam sitcom reaction beat — the men ogling the attractive woman. Functional but not especially inventive. It earns its place as setup for the following jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: So where are you from?

dialogue.speaker: New Roommate
dialogue.line: Ohio.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh cool. And what do your parents do?

dialogue.speaker: New Roommate
dialogue.line: My mom's a teacher and my dad's an accountant.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Nice, nice. So you ever been to New York before?

dialogue.speaker: New Roommate
dialogue.line: No, this is my first time.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Wow. So you're telling me you don't know ANYTHING about New York? You don't know where Times Square is? You don't know who the mayor is? You don't even know what a bagel is?

jokes.text: Ross asks if Joey interviewed Janine before asking her to move in; Joey reveals his entire interview was 'When can you move in?'
jokes.setup: Ross asks 'Did you interview her before you asked her to move in?' with the implication that Joey should have vetted her
jokes.punchline: 'What did you ask her?' / 'When can you move in?' — Joey's screening process was entirely about timing, not compatibility
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's cleaner jokes. The setup (did you vet her?) reasonably implies a list of normal questions; the reveal that Joey's only criterion was availability is perfectly economical and character-specific. Joey's priorities — a pretty woman, available immediately — could not be better captured in four words.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: When can you move in?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: That's it? That's the whole interview?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Well, I asked it different ways.

jokes.text: Monica sincerely thanks Joey for 'bringing her into our lives' regarding a gorgeous woman she has no personal stake in
jokes.setup: Ross and Chandler are clearly excited; Monica's reaction is unexpected
jokes.punchline: 'Thank you for bringing her into our lives.' — Monica's complete sincerity about a hot woman moving in nearby, treating it like a gift to the group
jokes.explanation: Monica's pragmatic acceptance of attractive women in the friend group, contrasted with the men's barely concealed excitement, is a solid character moment. Not exceptional but lands consistently.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: It's like living with a ghost. Except the ghost sleeps with you and knows all your secrets.

jokes.text: 'Down, boy.' / 'Oh, no, no, no. She's not my type. Not for me, she's not my type. She's too...' / 'Beautiful, tall, sexy, showing her stomach?' / 'Look at all the boxes!'
jokes.setup: Joey is visibly smitten with Janine; Monica tells him to calm down
jokes.punchline: Joey denies Janine is his type with increasingly hollow protests, then when Monica lists all Janine's attractive traits as Joey's supposed objections, he desperately pivots: 'Look at all the boxes!'
jokes.explanation: The pivot to 'Look at all the boxes!' is a genuinely funny non-sequitur escape hatch. Joey's denial crumbles in real time as Monica names every single thing he finds attractive. The desperation of the subject change lands well.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: It's hard not to flirt around attractive women.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Yeah, well you manage it around me just fine.

jokes.text: Ross argues against Joey dating Janine: 'If you date her, then I can't date her'
jokes.setup: Joey is told not to date his roommate because it's too complicated
jokes.punchline: Ross reveals his actual concern is entirely selfish — if Joey is dating her, Ross's own chances are eliminated
jokes.explanation: Ross's self-interest posing as advice is a solid character joke. His friends-code rationalization is instantly readable as pure self-interest. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I can't run with Phoebe.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Why not?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Because when she runs, she looks like a cross between a ostrich and a... and a little muppet.

jokes.text: Ross says imagining breaking up with someone you live with is like 'bumping into her at the supermarket' — 'Now imagine you live at the supermarket'
jokes.setup: Ross recalls a bad post-breakup supermarket encounter with Donna as an analogy for living with an ex
jokes.punchline: 'Now imagine you live at the supermarket.' — The extended metaphor snaps into place with satisfying economy
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest lines. The supermarket metaphor is structurally elegant — set up with enough specificity (Donna, the horror of the encounter) so that the payoff lands with real punch. It's relatable, economic, and the callback is used again later, making it a mini-running-gag. Good construction.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I kissed the Six Million Dollar Man poster.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: You mean like... 'We can rebuild him'?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No, no, no. His thing was 'We can rebuild him, we have the technology.'

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: That's... that's literally the same thing.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I know! But I kept singing it like 'The Rainbow Connection.'

jokes.text: Chandler admits it's hard to be around an attractive woman and not flirt — Monica points out she's around him all the time
jokes.setup: Chandler says flirting is his default around attractive women and he can't help it
jokes.punchline: 'You're around me all the time, and you don't flirt.' — Monica's self-deprecating observation; then 'A little sad about that, sweetie?' — Chandler's gentle counter-dig
jokes.explanation: A two-beat joke that works beautifully because both characters are self-aware. Monica's line sets a trap for herself (implying Chandler doesn't find her attractive), Chandler's response ('A little sad about that, sweetie?') gently flips it. The relationship dynamic — loving but able to tease — is captured perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh no, I can't run today. I have a terrible blister.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Monica, why did you make me wear those shoes?

jokes.text: 'You're around me all the time, and you don't flirt.' / [beat] / 'A little sad about that, sweetie?'
jokes.setup: Joey says it's hard to be around an attractive woman and not flirt — Monica points out he's around her all the time and doesn't flirt
jokes.punchline: Chandler gently asks if Monica is a 'little sad about that' — she inadvertently revealed she wishes Chandler flirted with her more
jokes.explanation: Beautifully economical relationship joke. Monica walks into it herself — her attempt to prove a point inadvertently reveals a mild insecurity in her relationship. Chandler's response is tender and funny simultaneously. 'A little sad about that, sweetie?' does enormous emotional and comedic work in seven words. Strong Mondler character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: It's ankle. Singular.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: And it might get worse.

jokes.text: Rachel sees how Phoebe runs and is horrified — Chandler describes it as 'like Kermit the Frog and the Six Million Dollar Man'
jokes.setup: Rachel has gone running with Phoebe and presumably returned traumatized; Chandler reports what he witnessed
jokes.punchline: 'She looks like Kermit the Frog and the Six Million Dollar Man.' — The specificity and incompatibility of the two references creates a genuinely funny visual
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines of the episode. The comparison is bizarre, specific, and vivid — the loose, floppy limbs of Kermit combined with the slow-motion heroics of the Six Million Dollar Man creates an immediately legible but absurd mental image. Highly quotable, memorable, and earns its place as the episode's signature joke. The specificity elevates it above a generic 'she runs funny' joke.

dialogue.speaker: Janine
dialogue.line: Joey, where are you? I thought you were helping me unpack!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm in here!

dialogue.speaker: Janine
dialogue.line: In where?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: In the box! Surprise!

jokes.text: Ross mentions Monica used to kiss the Six Million Dollar Man's poster every night — Monica immediately admits it
jokes.setup: Ross brings up the Six Million Dollar Man poster as a way to embarrass Monica
jokes.punchline: 'I used to do that too!' — Monica doesn't even try to deny it, confirming Ross's story with zero shame
jokes.explanation: A solid sibling-teasing beat. Monica's unashamed admission is funnier than a denial would be. Standard Friends ensemble callback structure.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Well, I mean, I'm a great roommate. I'm clean, I'm quiet, I pay my share of the rent...

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Oh, and I'm really good in bed.

jokes.text: Ross asks Monica if she also had the Six Million Dollar Man's album 'It's Not Easy Being Green' — which is Kermit the Frog's song
jokes.setup: Ross is teasing Monica about her childhood crush on the Six Million Dollar Man
jokes.punchline: 'Did you also have his album, "It's Not Easy Being Green"?' — which is Kermit's song, not the Six Million Dollar Man's, mixing the two references from Chandler's earlier description
jokes.explanation: A genuinely clever callback joke that rewards attention. Ross attributes Kermit's signature song to the Six Million Dollar Man — deliberately or innocently merging Chandler's two-part description. It works on multiple levels: as a callback to Chandler's line, as Ross being oblivious, and as an absurdist payoff. The construction is tight and the joke earns its punchline. Among the episode's best-written moments.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey Chandler, how you doin'?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What? Why are you looking at me like that?

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I don't know, man. I've got all this flirting energy built up and I gotta use it on somebody!

jokes.text: Rachel tells Phoebe she hurt herself running — but the lie is transparently obviously designed to avoid running with her again
jokes.setup: Rachel has told Phoebe Monica tripped her so she 'can't ever run again'
jokes.punchline: The scene plays as cringe — everyone can see Rachel is lying, including Phoebe, while Rachel thinks she's being subtle
jokes.explanation: A functional cringe beat — Rachel's transparent lie and Phoebe's knowing 'I'm not an idiot' response set up the later confrontation. Not especially funny on its own but serves the episode's B-plot.

dialogue.speaker: Janine
dialogue.line: I'm sorry about all my stuff hanging in the bathroom.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, no problem.

dialogue.speaker: Janine
dialogue.line: It's just my bras and my underwear, they take a long time to dry.

jokes.text: Phoebe corrects 'ankle' to 'we'll see' when Rachel says 'ankle' (singular)
jokes.setup: Rachel says 'I know. I'm sorry I hurt your ankle.' (singular)
jokes.punchline: 'Ankle. / We'll see.' — Phoebe implying she may have hurt more than one, delivered with ominous calm
jokes.explanation: Two words that do enormous work. The deadpan threat implied in 'We'll see' — which also implies Phoebe is cataloguing injuries — is a perfect Phoebe line. Maximum economy.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Oh my God, you two look exactly alike!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What? No, we don't!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yeah, you do. You both have that same 'Oh my God, what have we done?' look.

jokes.text: Ross pretends he didn't notice Joey had left and there's 'still one box left to unpack' — which contains Joey hiding inside
jokes.setup: Ross says Joey has gone home, then refers to 'one last box to unpack'
jokes.punchline: Joey leaps out of the box yelling 'I got you!' — having hidden himself inside to scare Ross; Ross screams
jokes.explanation: Classic physical comedy that works as a sight gag — a grown man hiding in a box to scare another grown man. The mismatch of childish behavior in a serious setting (moving day, new roommate) is funny. Execution-dependent but would land in the room.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You guys need a couple nickname. Like Brangelina.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: What would ours be?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Mondler.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That sounds like a skin condition.

jokes.text: Chandler announces Monica is working late so he's going to make the place 'spotless' and get her flowers — 'Who wouldn't want to live with me?'
jokes.setup: Chandler describes his wholesome domestic plans
jokes.punchline: 'Who wouldn't want to live with me?' — An earnest question that is about to be dramatically undercut by the chaos he'll create
jokes.explanation: Setup for the Monica's-apartment storyline. The irony of Chandler's self-congratulatory question being immediately answered by imminent disaster is functional foreshadowing comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Are you insane? Monica doesn't just care where things go - she has a system. A color-coded, alphabetized, geometrically organized system. Last week she reorganized the pantry by nutritional value. She once spent three hours arranging her spice rack by cuisine origin AND frequency of use. You put one thing back in the wrong place and she will know. She will KNOW.

jokes.text: Joey immediately answers 'Who wouldn't want to live with me?' with 'I don't'
jokes.setup: Chandler rhetorically asks 'Who wouldn't want to live with me?'
jokes.punchline: Joey's instant, matter-of-fact 'I don't' — not cruel, just honest; he's already chosen a hot Australian dancer instead
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy. Joey's response is two words that do maximum damage with minimum malice. It's not an insult; it's just the honest answer that happens to deflate Chandler completely. The juxtaposition of Chandler's pride and Joey's total lack of sentimentality is a great character moment.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Dude, I'm telling you, do not mess with Monica right now.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Why? What's wrong with her?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: She's in a mood. And when she's in a mood, she gets creative with her threats.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: How creative are we talking?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: She told me if I didn't do my laundry, she'd sit on me.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: That's... oddly specific and weirdly childish.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I know! That's what scared me!

jokes.text: Joey, testing out flirting techniques for Chandler, says 'How you doing?' at Ross — Ross immediately yells 'Get out!'
jokes.setup: Joey has 'built-up flirting energy' he doesn't know how to discharge; he tests his famous line on Ross
jokes.punchline: Ross's explosive 'Get out!' — the inappropriateness of flirting at a straight male friend, combined with Joey's signature catchphrase being deployed in the wrong context
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's most reliable crowd-pleasers. Joey's catchphrase being deployed at the wrong person in a moment of desperation is a great subversion of the running gag. Ross's instant, explosive rejection makes it. The character specificity is excellent — only Joey would have this problem, only Ross would react this way.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: My day was terrible. First, I spilled coffee all over myself. Then I got stuck in traffic for two hours. Then I found out they gave my shift to someone else.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I'm hanging up.

jokes.text: Janine recoils from Joey trying to touch her because she's 'all sweaty from the workout' — visual cringe moment of their first uncomfortable physical boundary
jokes.setup: Joey approaches Janine in what would normally be a flirtatious way
jokes.punchline: 'I didn't want you to touch me because I'm all sweaty from the workout' — Janine's polite rejection of physical contact disguised as practicality
jokes.explanation: A mild cringe beat that establishes Janine's boundary-setting without being funny enough to be a standout joke. It's scene-work rather than proper comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Okay, so the couch goes there, but that means the chair has to move to the other side.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: But if the chair moves there, then the table doesn't fit.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Right, so the table goes against the wall, which means the lamp has to go on the other side of the couch.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Okay, but now the TV can't see the couch.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: So we move the TV, which means we have to move the entertainment center.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Which blocks the window.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: So we close the curtains!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: There are no curtains, Mon. That's why we moved the chair in the first place.

jokes.text: Janine apologizes for her thongs hanging in the shower — 'my thongs are too delicate for the dryer'
jokes.setup: Joey is startled by something hanging in the shower
jokes.punchline: Janine explains her thong underwear is too delicate for the dryer — Joey's wide-eyed reaction is implied
jokes.explanation: A physical comedy beat that plays on Joey's predicament — he's trying NOT to be attracted to his roommate and she keeps doing things that are inadvertently provocative. Functional but not especially crafted.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Okay, okay, I have an idea. What if we... what if we pivot?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Pivot!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Pivot!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: PIVOT! PIVOT! PIVOT!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: It won't go! Why won't it go?! It's a chaise lounge, it should... Why won't anybody help me?!

jokes.text: Phoebe confronts Rachel for sneaking out to run alone — Rachel's excuse unravels in real time: 'I was actually just checking... to see... if I could run. And I can!'
jokes.setup: Phoebe saw Rachel grab her running shoes and sneak out early
jokes.punchline: Rachel's improvised excuse collapses mid-sentence into the logical absurdity that she was testing whether she could run — and she can
jokes.explanation: Rachel's specific cadence of a lie falling apart in real time is genuinely funny — the increasingly long pauses as she constructs the excuse live, then the triumphant 'And I can!' as if this solves everything. Good character work from Rachel.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I'm not even trying! It's like I'm a magnet, and women are steel. I don't do anything, they just come to me. It's a gift and a curse.

jokes.text: Cut to Monica and Chandler's apartment — the sight gag of Chandler and Ross clearly visible as a couple through the building, Phoebe's line: 'Couples who live together do start to look alike'
jokes.setup: Phoebe is at the window watching Chandler and Ross across the way
jokes.punchline: 'Couples who live together do start to look alike.' — Phoebe mistakes Ross and Chandler for a couple due to their domestic behavior
jokes.explanation: A quick observational joke playing on the classic 'couples grow to look alike' trope applied to two straight male friends doing housework together. The visual setup sells it.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey guys, how do I get women to stay away from me?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Just be yourself.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, it works for us.

jokes.text: Monica snapping at Chandler to 'say what you have to say and leave me alone' at work — then Phoebe notes they 'sound alike too'
jokes.setup: Chandler has apparently been near-Monica in domestic behavior; Monica is overheard being abrasive at work
jokes.punchline: 'Sound alike too.' — implying the Monica-Chandler partnership is making them equivalent in personality, specifically in Monica's bossiness
jokes.explanation: A quick extension of the previous beat. 'Sound alike too' as a two-word callback works efficiently, implying Monica's controlling manner is rubbing off on Chandler/being matched by the apartment dynamic.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I do not repel women! I've been married three times!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, that's not helping your case.

jokes.text: Phoebe calls the Monica/Chandler pairing 'Mondler'
jokes.setup: Phoebe is observing the couple from afar
jokes.punchline: 'So, Mondler...' — a portmanteau couple nickname years before it became a cultural norm, delivered with Phoebe's characteristic odd certainty
jokes.explanation: A deceptively sharp joke — the portmanteau couple nickname was not yet a pop culture cliché in 1999, making Phoebe feel ahead of the curve and genuinely quirky rather than performatively so. Highly quotable and rewatchable as a cultural artifact.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So Ross walks up to this girl at the dance, and he's like, 'Hey, did you know that the mating habits of the tree frog are actually fascinating?' And she just stares at him.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: It was a conversation starter!

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: At a *dance*, Ross. Not at a nature documentary.

jokes.text: Ross warns Chandler that Monica will freak out if he moves her stuff — Chandler dismisses it; Ross's 'Hello? Did you just meet Monica?' captures the absurdity
jokes.setup: Chandler insists Monica will appreciate the gesture and won't mind the rearrangement
jokes.punchline: 'Hello? Did you just meet Monica?' — Ross's exasperated appeal to Chandler's surely obvious knowledge of his girlfriend's personality
jokes.explanation: A reliable crowd-pleaser that uses Monica's established obsessive personality as the punchline. 'Did you just meet Monica?' is a quotable line that works because it invites the audience to side with Ross's exasperation.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I don't have an annoying habit.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh, you don't? What about that thing you do with your shoulder?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: What thing? I don't do anything with my shoulder.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: *does the shoulder thing repeatedly*

jokes.text: Ross says he lived with Monica for 16 years, then: 'She's going to sit on you'
jokes.setup: Ross is warning Chandler about Monica's reaction; Chandler remains dismissive
jokes.punchline: 'She's going to sit on you.' — An unexpectedly physical threat delivered with casual certainty by her own brother
jokes.explanation: The specific nature of the threat ('sit on you') is what makes this funny — it's not 'she'll be angry' but a weirdly specific sibling threat that implies a childhood history. Monica's weight used to be part of the show's backstory, which gives this line an extra layer. Delivered as obvious fact by her brother.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, it's not that they're girls. Nobody likes it when you talk about science.

jokes.text: Chandler responds to 'she's going to sit on you' with 'That probably won't hurt as much anymore'
jokes.setup: Ross threatens that Monica will 'sit on you' as a punishment
jokes.punchline: 'That probably won't hurt as much anymore.' — Chandler's reference to Monica's weight loss, delivered with enough affection and tact that it isn't cruel
jokes.explanation: A quick, well-calibrated callback. The joke works because it's NOT mean — Chandler isn't mocking Monica, he's making a neutral observation about her transformation that also happens to deflect the threat. The delivery would need to be light, but on the page it's a solid secondary beat.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Well, I'm glad we got that out in the open. I feel like a weight has been lifted off my shoulders.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, I feel like I've been hit by a truck.

jokes.text: Chandler calls Monica at work to prove he's fine — Monica immediately says 'Terrible... I might even kill someone tonight' — Chandler panics and talks her out of coming home early
jokes.setup: Chandler calls to reassure himself; Monica's work day has been terrible and she wants to come home
jokes.punchline: Chandler, who needs her NOT to come home, has to convince her to stay at the job she hates — 'It sounds like they need you there' / 'You're just hanging out with Ross? It's all good! Bye!'
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed irony — Chandler called to reassure himself that he had time, and in doing so learned he has no time at all. Monica's murderous mood adds stakes. The abrupt 'It's all good! Okay, bye!' as Chandler cuts the call early is a great panic button.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: I can't run outside, Phoebe. What if someone sees me?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: So?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: So? So I'd die of embarrassment!

jokes.text: After the call, Ross points out 'The phone was facing the other way' — revealing a tiny continuity error that Chandler now has to also fix
jokes.setup: Chandler has just panicked about putting everything back; Ross observes a detail
jokes.punchline: 'The phone was facing the other way.' — The realization that everything, even a phone's orientation, must be restored exactly
jokes.explanation: The escalating specificity of Monica's control-freakery is well-deployed here. Even the phone's facing becomes a problem — which neatly establishes the absurd depth of the task ahead and raises stakes comedically.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: The strangers don't matter.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: They don't matter? Phoebe, they have EYES!

jokes.text: Chandler tries to demonstrate the couch is in the right place by sitting to put his feet on the coffee table — it's clearly nowhere near it
jokes.setup: Chandler argues the couch is correctly placed 'in line with the carpet'
jokes.punchline: He sits and reaches for the coffee table — it's too far; his legs dangle uselessly in the wrong direction
jokes.explanation: A reliable physical comedy beat. Chandler's attempt to demonstrate normalcy only highlights how wrong everything is. The visual of his feet dangling uselessly would get a good reaction in the studio.

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I run like the wind. No rules, no structure, just pure freedom. When I was a kid, I had to run away from Satan all the time, so now I just run for the joy of it.

jokes.text: Joey walks in on the apartment chaos: 'What the hell's going on over here?' — then immediately: 'Monica's gonna kill you!'
jokes.setup: Chandler and Ross are surrounded by displaced furniture; it's visually chaotic
jokes.punchline: Joey's instant assessment that Monica's going to kill Chandler — with no hesitation, no comfort offered
jokes.explanation: Joey's reaction beats are always funny because he delivers verdicts with absolute certainty and no cushioning. The immediate shift from 'what happened?' to 'you're dead' is very Joey. Functional rather than exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Wait, Satan?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Yeah, my father is Satan.

jokes.text: Chandler asks Ross and Joey for help repelling women — 'You guys repel women all the time!'
jokes.setup: Chandler needs to make himself unattractive to Janine to avoid romantic complications
jokes.punchline: 'You guys repel women all the time!' — Chandler's backhanded compliment that is also a devastating insult about Ross and Joey's dating track record
jokes.explanation: A smartly constructed double-meaning compliment — Chandler is asking for expertise in something they're presumably bad at, which is itself an insult. The setup-and-reveal structure works well.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: So where should we put the couch?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: It doesn't matter. I'm never getting married anyway.

jokes.text: Ross's woman-repelling technique: talking about the Irish potato famine
jokes.setup: Chandler asks what Ross and Joey do that repels women — Ross describes walking up to a girl he liked at a dance
jokes.punchline: '...and talked about the Irish potato famine.' — Ross's first-date topic is a 19th-century agricultural catastrophe
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes because the specificity is perfect. Not just 'history' or 'boring topics' — the Irish potato famine. It's specific enough to be absurd, historically real enough to make Ross's academic nature feel authentic, and completely incompatible with romance. Pure character-driven comedy. The specificity is what elevates this from a 6 to an 8.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Why would Ross be naked?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: He's... cleaning himself.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Cleaning himself? He's in the living room!

jokes.text: Joey's woman-repelling technique: a specific awkward gesture he makes after talking — described as making a sound/gesture that the script implies is physically demonstrated
jokes.setup: Ross says Joey wasn't much better at the dance — 'After everything he said, he'd go..'
jokes.punchline: Joey apparently performs a cringe sound or gesture — Chandler's immediate reaction: 'Monica doesn't like that either. I should stop doing that.' implies it's a universally unpleasant affectation
jokes.explanation: A visual/physical gag that the transcript can only partially capture. The humor is in the implied physical performance and in Chandler's instant self-recognition ('I should stop doing that') — the admission that he shares this quality. Strong rewatch value since the physical bit would be visible.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Why are you naked?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I'm not naked. I'm just between clothing.

jokes.text: Ross notes 'Girls don't like it when I start talking about science' — Joey: 'That's not specific to girls'
jokes.setup: Ross is listing things women find off-putting about him
jokes.punchline: 'That's not specific to girls.' — Joey's flat correction that Ross's science talk repels everyone, not just women
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best-constructed jokes. The setup is Ross's self-aware confession, but the punchline brutally expands the scope — it's not a gender issue, it's a Ross issue. Joey's delivery as deadpan fact rather than insult makes it land harder. Maximum economy (five words) for maximum damage. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: It's a medical condition! I have a very rare... skin thing.

jokes.text: They don't like it when you correct their grammar / explain why your jokes are funny / keep asking if they like you
jokes.setup: Ross and Joey are cataloguing their woman-repelling behaviors for Chandler
jokes.punchline: Three rapid-fire confessions, each more painfully recognizable than the last — correcting grammar, explaining jokes, asking 'do you like me?' on a loop
jokes.explanation: A well-paced trio of observational jokes that work through accumulation. Each one is relatable (we've all met that person) while also being character-specific to Ross and Joey. The escalation from annoying (grammar correction) to desperate (asking if they like you) tracks well.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I have the same problem Chandler had.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh, you can't... you can't get it up?

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No! No, I didn't say that!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh, well Chandler couldn't either.

jokes.text: Chandler: 'Man, I am so lucky I have Monica.' Joey: 'I'm never gonna find love again.'
jokes.setup: The woman-repelling list has been going on; both men are reflecting
jokes.punchline: Chandler's conclusion (grateful he escaped the dating pool) contrasts with Joey's sudden existential despair — despite Joey being the one who finds dating easiest
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of Chandler's relief with Joey's melodrama is funny precisely because Joey, of all people, would logically have the least to worry about. The irony is well-calibrated — Joey having a crisis of romantic confidence after cataloguing his own flaws is a good character moment.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Wait, what medical condition? Chandler, what are you talking about?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I don't have a medical condition.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Then why did you say you did?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I didn't!

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: You totally did. You said something about a... a thing. A medical thing.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Ross, I think you're making this up.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I am not making this up! Monica heard it too!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Actually, I wasn't really listening.

jokes.text: Rachel finally admits to Phoebe why she didn't want to run with her — trails off: 'The way that you run is just a little...'
jokes.setup: Rachel has been asked to tell the truth about why she avoided running with Phoebe
jokes.punchline: Rachel cannot bring herself to finish the sentence — the unspoken criticism hanging in the air is funnier than any specific word would be
jokes.explanation: Rachel's social politeness creating its own cringe comedy — she can't even finish the gentle criticism. The gap between what she's trying to say and what she can bring herself to say is well-played. Good character work.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: You want a beer?

dialogue.speaker: Janine
dialogue.line: For I.

jokes.text: Rachel explains she was embarrassed because 'People were looking at us.' Phoebe: 'Why do you care?' Rachel: 'Because they're people!' Phoebe: 'People you don't know and will never see again.' Rachel: 'Yes, but still they are people... with eyes.'
jokes.setup: Rachel is mortified by strangers' reactions to Phoebe's running; Phoebe doesn't understand
jokes.punchline: 'Yes, but still they are people... with eyes.' — Rachel's escalating justification lands on the most basic anatomical observation as if it explains everything
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best exchanges. Rachel's logic collapses to its most fundamental level — 'they have eyes' — as if sight alone makes strangers' opinions matter. The beat-pause before 'with eyes' is what makes it land. It's perfect Rachel: style-obsessed, superficial, and yet completely sincere. Highly quotable and character-defining.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Hey, you want to split a pizza?

dialogue.speaker: Janine
dialogue.line: I know how to eat pizza, okay? I've been eating pizza since before you were even born!

jokes.text: Phoebe starts to say she wasn't embarrassed running next to 'Miss...' then trails off — an implied callback to someone in Rachel's past or a compliment she can't quite deliver
jokes.setup: Phoebe is pushing back on Rachel's embarrassment — implying Phoebe was not embarrassed to run next to Rachel despite Rachel's potential for embarrassing her
jokes.punchline: Phoebe can't finish the sentence either — both women are trapped by their inability to complete diplomatic yet pointed sentences
jokes.explanation: A structural mirror of Rachel's trailing sentence — both women unable to complete their criticisms. Thematically neat but doesn't land as hard as joke 49 because the first trailing sentence was funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Look, I know what's happening here. You're attracted to me. I mean, who could blame you? I'm Joey Tribbiani. I've got the looks, I've got the charm, I've got the... well, let's be honest, I've got it all.

jokes.text: Phoebe tells Rachel she's 'uptight' — Rachel furiously insists 'I am not uptight, man' — the word 'man' deployed by Rachel undermining her protest
jokes.setup: Phoebe calls Rachel 'uptight' about strangers' opinions
jokes.punchline: Rachel's heated denial 'I am not uptight, man' — Rachel trying to sound casual by saying 'man' is itself uptight
jokes.explanation: Rachel's failed attempt to sound laid-back ('man') while being visibly wound up is a nicely layered joke. The self-undermining quality of the protest is well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: I can't date her. She's like my sister.

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Yeah, and I can't date her either. She's like my sister.

jokes.text: Phoebe explains she runs 'like I did when I was a kid... because that's the only way it's fun' — referencing running away from Satan (the neighbor's dog)
jokes.setup: Phoebe describes her free-spirited approach to running — 'like you were running towards the swings or running away from Satan'
jokes.punchline: 'The neighbor's dog.' — The reveal that Satan was a dog, delivered as a simple clarification, retroactively makes Phoebe's childhood sound both vivid and slightly traumatic
jokes.explanation: The episode's single best joke. Phoebe's matter-of-fact parenthetical 'The neighbor's dog' after 'running away from Satan' is a masterclass in character comedy. It works on every level: (1) The escalation from normal (swings) to supernatural (Satan) to mundane (the dog) is a perfect three-beat structure. (2) It's completely Phoebe — her casual relationship with the supernatural, her unusual childhood, her sincerity. (3) The clarification itself implies that this needed clarifying, that in Phoebe's world, Satan is a reasonable reference point. Highly quotable, deeply character-specific, and structurally perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: Janine, I've been thinking about us, and I realize we have this great friendship, and if we started dating it could ruin everything. We work together, we see each other every day, and the stakes are just too high. Plus, you're my dance partner, and that's a sacred thing. I mean, look at all the complications that could arise—

dialogue.speaker: Janine
dialogue.line: Joey, I'm not interested in you.

jokes.text: In the middle of furniture chaos, Joey absently asks 'Is this in the right place?' — Chandler: 'Who cares? I repel women.'
jokes.setup: Joey holds a piece of furniture; Chandler is preoccupied with his failed flirting repulsion plan
jokes.punchline: 'Who cares? I repel women.' — Chandler has completely dissociated from the furniture crisis, now only focused on the Janine situation
jokes.explanation: A quick mid-crisis pivot joke that gets a good laugh from Chandler's parallel preoccupations colliding. The sudden tonal shift from 'furniture' to 'existential woman-repelling' is well-timed.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: She rejected me! Can you believe that? Me! Joey Tribbiani!

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: But that's okay, because I was testing her. Yeah, I wanted to see if she was the type of girl who would stick around even when I'm being deliberately repulsive. Turns out she's not. Her loss!

jokes.text: Ross yells 'You can't come in here! Ross is naked!' to block Janine from entering
jokes.setup: Janine approaches the apartment; Ross needs to prevent her from seeing the furniture chaos (and apparently is or will be naked for the repelling plan)
jokes.punchline: 'Ross is naked!' — Ross referring to himself in the third person while also announcing something deeply alarming to a near-stranger
jokes.explanation: Third-person self-announcement is always a good structural joke, and the content (nakedness) adds absurdist urgency. The scene escalates well and the third-person usage feels organically panicked.

dialogue.speaker: Joey
dialogue.line: How you doin'?

jokes.text: Chandler explains he couldn't say he was naked 'because she's allowed to see me naked' — the logical problem of nakedness being a repellent
jokes.setup: Ross announced HIS nakedness to block Janine; Chandler explains why he couldn't say the same
jokes.punchline: 'I couldn't say I was naked, because she's allowed to see me naked.' — The paradox of Chandler's relationship status making nudity useless as a deterrent
jokes.explanation: A smart logic-of-the-situation joke. The implication — Monica has seen Chandler naked, so it doesn't deter anyone — creates an absurd relationship-status hierarchy of nudity-as-weapon. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God, Phoebe, how do you run like that?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Well, you just let your body be free. Feel the wind, become one with the pavement.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Okay, I'm gonna try it.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Oh my God! Oh my God, I feel it! I feel the connection to everything!

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Phoebe, this is amazing! We should all just run like this!

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: I know, right?

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: From now on, I'm never running normally again. This is the only way to live!

jokes.text: Monica asks why Ross is naked — Ross: 'I had to show Chandler something.' — a deliberately unexplained answer
jokes.setup: Monica has arrived at some point and wants to know why Ross is naked in her apartment
jokes.punchline: 'I had to show Chandler something.' — Ross's vague, slightly horrifying explanation that explains nothing and implies something disturbing
jokes.explanation: Perfectly vague. 'I had to show Chandler something' is funnier because it's never explained — the audience's imagination does more work than any specific answer would. The nonchalance of the delivery makes it land harder. Good economy and strong misdirection.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Why is there a horse in the middle of Central Park?

dialogue.speaker: Phoebe
dialogue.line: Oh, that's just Kevin. He comes here to think.

jokes.text: Joey asks 'Naked? I guess I have... a "guy" problem.' Then: 'Is it the same thing Chandler had?'
jokes.setup: Ross and Chandler are trying to usher Monica back out; Joey is processing the nakedness
jokes.punchline: 'Is it the same thing Chandler had?' — Joey implying Chandler has had a similar mysterious 'guy problem' requiring nudity, adding a second layer of implication
jokes.explanation: An extension of the vague 'guy problem' joke. Joey's reference to Chandler's past 'thing' implies a history of embarrassing medical situations, adding comic depth while maintaining plausible deniability.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Chandler, everything in this apartment is different. The furniture, the decorations, even the lighting. What is going on?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: I was going for romantic. You know, candlelight, soft music, rose petals... I wanted to sweep you off your feet.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: By completely rearranging our apartment without asking?

dialogue.speaker: Chandler
dialogue.line: Could I BE any more thoughtful?

jokes.text: Ross guesses he has 'a guy problem' — implying something private — and Joey asks 'Is it the same thing Chandler had?'
jokes.setup: Ross is trying to explain why he was naked to Chandler
jokes.punchline: Joey asks if it's 'the same thing Chandler had' — implying Chandler has had a mysterious 'guy problem' that required nudity to demonstrate
jokes.explanation: The vagueness is the joke — 'guy problem' and 'the same thing Chandler had' are both deliberately non-specific in a way that lets the audience's imagination supply the worst possible interpretation. Good innuendo structure.

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Oh Chandler, that's so sweet!

dialogue.speaker: Monica
dialogue.line: Wait, is that Ross? Oh my God, put some clothes on! Do you know how many things you've sat on in this apartment?

jokes.text: In the rush to get Monica out, someone reveals 'There's still some of Chandler's medicine in the bathroom' — deeply ambiguous
jokes.setup: Everyone is trying to push Monica back out the door; a reason is needed
jokes.punchline: 'There's still some of Chandler's medicine in the bathroom.' — What medicine? For what? The implication is worse than any answer
jokes.explanation: The running gag of Chandler's mysterious ailment culminates in 'medicine in the bathroom' — deliberately vague enough to imply something embarrassing. The cumulative effect of the three-joke sequence about the 'guy problem' is funnier than any individual piece.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: I mean, think about it. Computers have become such an integral part of our lives. We pour our consciousness into them, and in a way, they become an extension of ourselves.

dialogue.speaker: Janine
dialogue.line: That's... actually kind of beautiful, Ross.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: Right? So when I look at you, I see a computer. And I want to pour my consciousness into you.

dialogue.speaker: Janine
dialogue.line: Okay, that's creepy.

jokes.text: Ross's brilliant plan: use apartment photos from the photo album to restore everything to its original position
jokes.setup: Chandler is desperate to restore Monica's apartment to its exact original configuration
jokes.punchline: Ross's revelation: 'The photo album! There were millions of pictures of the apartment in the photo album. We just match everything to the pictures!' — the implication being that Monica has obsessively documented her apartment's exact configuration
jokes.explanation: A great character joke about Monica — the punchline isn't just 'use photos,' it's the implication that Monica has taken 'millions of pictures of the apartment.' The joke confirms everything we believe about Monica's obsessive documentation while also being a satisfying plot solution. Great character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: It's like... you're the server, and I'm the client trying to establish a connection.

dialogue.speaker: Rachel
dialogue.line: Ross, that's the least romantic thing I've ever heard.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: No, wait! I'm still buffering my feelings for you!

jokes.text: Chandler, trying to repel Janine, corrects her grammar: 'Don't you mean "for whom"?' when she says 'I've got some beer for you'
jokes.setup: Chandler is deploying the repelling techniques from Ross and Joey's list; Janine offers beer
jokes.punchline: 'Don't you mean "for whom"?' — Chandler putting Ross's grammar-correction technique into action, it's immediately stilted and off-putting
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback payoff — we've been told grammar correction is a repellent, and now we see it in action. 'Don't you mean "for whom"?' is funny both as an execution of the plan and as a Chandler joke (he's good with words, so this is actually within his skillset, which is funnier than if it were awkward for him). Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Ross
dialogue.line: So, uh, I was thinking... you know how computers have those user-friendly interfaces? Well, I think you and I should have a very user-friendly interface.

dialogue.speaker: Janine
dialogue.line: I'm going to go... fold some clothes. In another room. Far away from you.

jokes.text: Janine pauses, then just says 'Sure.' — the perfect response to Chandler's grammar correction
jokes.setup: Chandler has just pedantically corrected Janine's grammar about 'for whom'
jokes.punchline: Janine's flat 'Sure.' — she neither takes offense nor engages; her total non-reaction deflates Chandler's repelling attempt immediately
jokes.explanation: One word doing the work of a paragraph. Janine's 'Sure' is the funniest possible response because it neither accepts nor rejects the correction — it's total indifference, which is the worst outcome for Chandler's repelling strategy. Economy is 9/10.

jokes.text: Chandler deploys the potato famine technique: 'I'm depressed about that Irish potato famine'
jokes.setup: Janine asks if something is wrong; Chandler has been acting strangely
jokes.punchline: 'Yeah. I'm depressed about that Irish potato famine.' — Chandler directly applying Ross's proven woman-repelling technique
jokes.explanation: The best callback of the episode. The Irish potato famine joke was already funny in isolation; seeing Chandler deploy it as a deliberate strategy elevates it. The fact that he says 'that Irish potato famine' — using the definite article as if it's a current, pressing concern — is perfect. Highly quotable and structurally excellent.

jokes.text: Chandler's big speech to Janine: 'You're hot. I'm lovable. Clearly there's a vibe going on between us. But we're roommates and it's a huge mistake.'
jokes.setup: Chandler has decided to address the supposed mutual attraction directly and honestly
jokes.punchline: His self-assessment — 'I'm lovable' — in a list with 'You're hot' is an absurd contrast; also the entire speech assumes a mutuality that doesn't exist
jokes.explanation: Chandler's self-classification as 'lovable' (vs. 'hot') while assuming Janine shares his attraction is a nicely observed piece of self-delusion. The whole speech sets up the brutal rejection to follow.

jokes.text: Janine reveals she doesn't like Chandler 'like that' — 'I think you're really sweet. But I'm not interested in you like that.'
jokes.setup: Chandler has built up to a dramatic confrontation about their mutual attraction
jokes.punchline: Janine's gentle rejection reveals the entire premise was false — she was never interested in him; Chandler's whole elaborate repelling plan was unnecessary
jokes.explanation: The structural payoff of the entire Chandler/Janine subplot. Everything he did — the grammar correction, the potato famine, the nakedness plan, the speech — was based on a false premise. The irony that his efforts to repel her were entirely redundant is a satisfying comedic inversion. Good construction.

jokes.text: Chandler, rejected, insists: 'It's because I was trying to repel you. Right? Believe me, you'd feel a lot different if I turned it on.'
jokes.setup: Janine has just clearly and kindly rejected Chandler
jokes.punchline: Chandler's desperate attribution of the rejection to his own deliberate repelling strategy — 'you'd feel a lot different if I turned it on' — a spectacular piece of self-delusion
jokes.explanation: Chandler's coping mechanism — reframing clear rejection as evidence of his own successful plan — is both very funny and very true to character. The phrase 'turned it on' is delusional in the best way. Great character integration.

jokes.text: Chandler, to prove he 'has it,' deploys his 'How you doing?' at Janine — she's underwhelmed
jokes.setup: Chandler insists he can be attractive if he 'turns it on'; Janine is skeptical
jokes.punchline: Chandler uses Joey's signature 'How you doing?' — which only works for Joey — and Janine responds 'I'm okay. What?' — she doesn't even register it as a flirt
jokes.explanation: A great callback that layers multiple jokes: (1) Chandler steals Joey's signature line, (2) it completely fails to work without Joey's delivery/energy, (3) Janine's baffled 'What?' shows she doesn't even parse it as flirtation. The transferability (or lack thereof) of Joey's charisma is a lovely theme. Strong character integration and a crowd-pleasing callback.

jokes.text: Janine's reaction to Chandler's failed 'How you doing?' — 'Oh, dear God!' — she finally registers what he's been doing
jokes.setup: Chandler has been trying to demonstrate his attractiveness with Joey's line
jokes.punchline: 'Oh, dear God!' — Janine's belated horror as the full picture of Chandler's behavior clicks into place
jokes.explanation: A delayed reaction beat that works because of the gap between what Chandler thinks he's doing and what Janine sees. The 'Oh, dear God' is the right level of horrified for the situation.

jokes.text: Rachel joins Phoebe running in the park and runs Phoebe's wild way — 'I feel so free and so graceful!'
jokes.setup: Rachel has been convinced by Phoebe's philosophy to try running 'like a kid'
jokes.punchline: Rachel converts entirely and runs the same crazy way — 'You don't care if people stare. It's only a second. Then you're gone!' Her transformation from uptight to wild is complete
jokes.explanation: The visual payoff of the episode's B-plot. Rachel's conversion to Phoebe-running is a physical comedy moment that the transcript only partially captures — the audience would see Jennifer Aniston running in the same absurd Kermit/Six Million Dollar Man style. Good resolution with warmth.

jokes.text: 'Watch out for the horse.' — delivered as Rachel is mid-run
jokes.setup: Rachel and Phoebe are running joyfully through the park
jokes.punchline: 'Watch out for the horse.' — Implying a horse is suddenly in the path; the mundane danger introduced into an already absurd scene
jokes.explanation: Four words that land perfectly. The timing (mid-joyful-run), the nonchalance of delivery, and the absurdity of a horse being the specific hazard makes this a standout moment. Central Park has horse-drawn carriages, so it's grounded, but the delivery makes it feel like the most natural thing in the world. Near-perfect economy.

jokes.text: Monica returns and immediately clocks that everything is different — 'Why is everything different?'
jokes.setup: Chandler and Ross have frantically tried to restore the apartment using the photos; they think they've succeeded
jokes.punchline: Monica's instant perception of wrongness — 'Why is everything different?' — before anyone has said a word
jokes.explanation: Monica's radar for her own apartment is a great character-based payoff. The joke is that all their effort was for nothing — she sees it immediately. Well-earned given the whole subplot, though the setup did most of the work.

jokes.text: Chandler's attempt to deflect with 'I don't see anything different... other than the fact that the room got brighter when you came into it'
jokes.setup: Monica has immediately noticed everything is wrong; Chandler tries to defuse with flattery
jokes.punchline: The corny romantic compliment ('room got brighter') is a transparent deflection that makes everything worse by being so obviously a tactic
jokes.explanation: A functional deflection joke — the cliché of the flattery dodge — but not particularly original. Gets a smile from the audience recognition of the tactic.

jokes.text: Monica lists exactly what's wrong: 'The end table is wrong, the couch looks bizarre, and don't even get me started on the refrigerator magnets'
jokes.setup: Monica is cataloguing the differences in her apartment
jokes.punchline: '...and don't even get me started on the refrigerator magnets.' — The escalation to magnets implies a level of obsessive awareness that goes beyond reasonable human perception
jokes.explanation: The escalation to refrigerator magnets is excellent character writing. It implies Monica has a canonical arrangement for even the smallest items in her kitchen. The 'don't even get me started' construction makes it funnier by promising more specificity that we don't get.

jokes.text: Monica has a surprisingly gracious reaction to Chandler's confession — then immediately asks 'Did Ross sit anywhere while he was naked?'
jokes.setup: Monica has accepted Chandler's apology with unusual grace; the scene seems to be resolving warmly
jokes.punchline: 'Did Ross sit anywhere while he was naked?' — Monica's true concern, the first thing she asks after the emotional resolution
jokes.explanation: The best joke of the episode and among the finest Monica jokes in the series. The structure is impeccable: (1) the warm reconciliation lulls the audience into thinking the scene is over, (2) the pivot to the REAL concern — naked Ross's contact with her furniture — is both a perfect character beat and a devastating subversion. Monica's priorities are revealed: she can forgive Chandler's good-faith gesture, but she cannot let the naked-Ross-furniture question go unanswered. This is the kind of joke that becomes a series touchstone. The specificity ('sit anywhere') is what makes it perfect rather than just good.

jokes.text: Monica, after forgiving Chandler beautifully, asks: 'Did Ross sit anywhere while he was naked?'
jokes.setup: Monica has just had a sweet, generous moment forgiving Chandler for the apartment disaster
jokes.punchline: The warm moment is immediately punctured by Monica's practical concern: did naked Ross sit on her furniture
jokes.explanation: The best joke in the episode. The structure is exquisite: Monica has just been generous, warm, and understanding — a lovely character moment — and then she pivots IMMEDIATELY to the most Monica possible follow-up concern. 'Did Ross sit anywhere while he was naked?' is both completely in character and a perfect callback to the nakedness subplot. The timing (the sweetness is barely over before this lands) makes it devastating. High quotability — the line works completely out of context. Iconic Mondler moment.

jokes.text: Ross concludes the computer speech with: 'Janine, do you know what we're doing right now? You and I, we're interfacing.'
jokes.setup: Ross has just explained how computers and human brains could interface; he applies the metaphor to himself and Janine
jokes.punchline: 'We're interfacing.' — Ross using a cold technical/computer term as a seduction line, completely unaware of how unsexy it is
jokes.explanation: The perfect button on the entire episode. 'We're interfacing' as a flirtation line encapsulates everything about Ross: his academic instincts, his inability to read a room, his sincere belief that intellectual engagement is romantic. The word 'interfacing' is precisely wrong enough — clinical, robotic, impersonal — to be a devastating punchline. Janine's immediately departure confirms its efficacy as a repellent without a single word needed. Highly quotable and character-defining for Ross.

jokes.text: Janine's immediate 'I gotta go.' after 'We're interfacing'
jokes.setup: Ross has just told Janine they're 'interfacing'
jokes.punchline: Janine's instant, flat exit line — 'I gotta go.' — the definitive verdict on Ross's conversational appeal
jokes.explanation: Three words that serve as the episode's closing punctuation. The speed of Janine's departure is what sells it — no hesitation, no polite excuse, just immediate evacuation. Perfect economy as the final beat.

tmdb_overview: Now roommates Phoebe and Rachel decide to start running together, but Rachel is embarrassed by Phoebe's odd running style. Joey finds a sexy new female roommate and tries very hard not to flirt with her. Meanwhile, Chandler decides to surprise Monica by cleaning the apartment, but forgets where everything goes. Ross tries to help him remedy the situation.
insight: Uneven character comedy carries a below-average episode through gentle escalation beats.
